description: Pure-Java full-stack framework: Java UI compiled for the browser by TeaVM, binary RPC over a persistent WebSocket, and EclipseStore object-graph persistence. You write no JavaScript, JSON, REST routes or SQL.
rules: Before you write anything, read the page for the task and do not rebuild what exists. The full documentation for this version is in the same jar as this file, under META-INF/zeroz4j/docs/ (the docs/ folder of the repository, same layout), and META-INF/zeroz4j/docs/llms.txt lists every page. The rules below name the page for each task.

Before you build a screen or a component: read META-INF/zeroz4j/docs/UI_COMPONENTS.md and the list 'Components that already exist' at the end of this file, then look for the same thing in the examples (META-INF/zeroz4j/docs/examples/index.md says which example shows what; the example sources are in the repository, not in the jar). Use the name common software uses, and use the component that exists.

Before you write a remote call that can take long (an AI model, a report, an import, anything that can pass 30 seconds): read META-INF/zeroz4j/docs/guides/slow-calls.md and use SlowCall. The rule on the 30-second request timeout in this file says why, and the section 'An RMI call never returns' in META-INF/zeroz4j/docs/guides/troubleshooting.md covers a call that is already failing.

Before you change or add a class that is stored: read META-INF/zeroz4j/docs/guides/persistence.md, including its section 'Observed behavior', and META-INF/zeroz4j/docs/store-modes.md. Enlisting does not cascade, enums are stored by position, and deleted data stays in the files.
When nothing happens on screen, or a call returns nothing, read META-INF/zeroz4j/docs/guides/troubleshooting.md before you read the code. Most of the silent cases are listed there by symptom.

Before you write a server's main class or change how it starts: read META-INF/zeroz4j/docs/guides/starting-the-server.md. For Vidocq read META-INF/zeroz4j/docs/guides/vidocq-server.md, and for packaging a runnable application read META-INF/zeroz4j/docs/guides/packaging.md.
Before you write sign-in, roles or tenant scoping: read META-INF/zeroz4j/docs/guides/security-auth.md. For OpenID Connect read META-INF/zeroz4j/docs/guides/oidc-auth.md and do not write a provider.

Before you accept a file: read META-INF/zeroz4j/docs/guides/file-uploads.md. Files never travel as RMI arguments. Before you play a recording or video, or show another page: read META-INF/zeroz4j/docs/guides/media.md and use AudioPlayer, VideoPlayer and EmbeddedFrame rather than an audio, video or iframe element of your own.
Before you add a page or a link between pages: read META-INF/zeroz4j/docs/ROUTING.md. Do not write your own navigation, spinner or history handling.
Before you write a test of a server: read META-INF/zeroz4j/docs/guides/testing.md. Use TestServer and TestConnection rather than a mock of the transport.

Before you choose how state moves between server and screens (signal, event, LiveSync or RMI): read META-INF/zeroz4j/docs/decide/index.md. For the classes that cross the wire read META-INF/zeroz4j/docs/guides/data-models.md, and for what is not supported read META-INF/zeroz4j/docs/reference/limitations.md.

Before you write a form or validation: read META-INF/zeroz4j/docs/guides/ui-forms-and-validation.md and META-INF/zeroz4j/docs/VALIDATION.md. For keyboard and naming of controls read META-INF/zeroz4j/docs/guides/ui-keyboard-and-naming.md, and for what sits above what read META-INF/zeroz4j/docs/guides/ui-layering.md.
Before you add a language, a number or date format, or an installable application: read META-INF/zeroz4j/docs/guides/language.md, or META-INF/zeroz4j/docs/PWA.md for installing.

Design rule: every RMI call has a 30 second limit. The default of WasmRmiClient.setRequestTimeout is 30 seconds, and a call still unanswered then fails on the client with RequestTimeoutException, whose message is 'The server did not answer in time. Try again.'. The server keeps working and may finish; only the answer is lost. So do not make work that waits on an AI model, a report, an import or anything else that can pass 30 seconds into one plain remote call that returns the result. Use a slow call (0.11.0+). Declare the service method as SlowCall<T> writeReport(...). In the implementation, @Inject com.zeroz4j.server.SlowCalls slowCalls and return slowCalls.start(key, job -> work). On the client call the stub as usual and read call.state() inside an Effect: running with percent() and progressText(), finished with value(), failed with message(), canceled. The key names the work per caller: starting a running key joins it, starting an ended key runs it again. After a page reload SlowCall.find(key) finds the work and starts nothing. job.progress(percent, text) reports progress, call.cancel() interrupts the work and sets job.isCanceled(). The work runs with the caller's RmiRequestContext except getSessionId(), which is null. The work belongs to the signed-in user within the tenant, or to the browser id when anonymous, and it survives a reconnect and a reload; a result is kept 60 minutes (zeroz.slowcall.keepMinutes). zeroz.slowcall.maxMinutes (default 0, no limit) stops work past that time, frees its running slot even if it ignores the interrupt, and shows 'The work took too long.'. Results are in memory, so a server restart loses them and the browser shows a sentence. Do not write a pending state, a result store, polling, or a thread that reports through a signal for this. Raising setRequestTimeout moves the limit for every call in the browser at once (0 turns it off) and leaves the person looking at a screen with nothing on it, so treat it as a stopgap. See META-INF/zeroz4j/docs/guides/slow-calls.md.

Theme: call Theme.start() once in main (com.zeroz4j.ui.theme.Theme). It stores light, dark or system in localStorage, sets data-theme on the html element, follows the operating system live, and the server shell sets it before the first paint. Read Theme.choice() and Theme.showing() (read-only signals) in an Effect; choose with Theme.choose(Theme.Choice.X); own DaisyUI theme names with Theme.configure(light, dark) before start(). Use ThemeController for the sun and moon button and ThemeSelector for Light, Dark, System on a settings screen; never build your own and never put data-theme on body, where it overrides html. Application CSS that follows the theme needs two selectors: :root[data-theme="dark"] and @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root:not([data-theme]) }. See the section 'Light, dark and system' in META-INF/zeroz4j/docs/UI_COMPONENTS.md.

A sizing class on a Checkbox or Toggle (min-h-*, h-*, w-*, size-*) is applied to the row around the box and its caption, not to the input, so the row gets taller or wider and the box keeps its shape. getElement() is still the input; getOuterElement() is the row. Make the box itself larger with setThemeSize(ThemeSize.LG). When the Checkbox has a caption (withLabel), the caption is a label tied to the box, so clicking the words ticks it.

Client code and the shared module are compiled for the browser by TeaVM, which has its own class library, while javac in mvn compile and mvn test-compile sees the whole JDK 21. So code can pass the quick check and fail the browser build, and a generated project's mvn compile does not run the browser build at all (run mvn install, as the build rule says). Checked by a real browser compile on TeaVM 0.15.0, each of these fails there with 'was not found': String.lines(), String.indent(int), String.transform(Function), StringBuilder.repeat(CharSequence, int), Locale.forLanguageTag(String), Thread.ofVirtual(), Thread.startVirtualThread(Runnable), and the classes CompletableFuture, Executors, ReentrantLock, ReentrantReadWriteLock, CountDownLatch, Semaphore, ConcurrentLinkedQueue and MessageDigest. In the DOM API of TeaVM 0.15.0, DOMTokenList (classList) has toggle(String) only, so toggle(String, boolean) does not exist; call add or remove by the condition. These compile in the browser: records, sealed types, pattern switch, record patterns, text blocks, String.formatted, Stream.toList, List.getFirst, List.reversed, Math.clamp, Thread, ConcurrentHashMap, AtomicReference and java.time formatting. Server modules are not compiled by TeaVM and are not affected. Add an entry here only after a browser compile has failed on it.
ZeroZ Stack requires JDK 21 or later. Client code is written in Java and compiled for the browser by TeaVM, so only TeaVM-supported JDK APIs are available in client modules.

ZeroZ Stack is published to Maven Central under groupId com.zeroz4j, and this rule list describes version 0.11.0. Import com.zeroz4j:zerozstack-bom as a POM dependency in dependencyManagement, then declare zerozstack-server-core, zerozstack-client, zerozstack-shared-api, zerozstack-ui-components and zerozstack-store-eclipsestore without versions. Add zerozstack-server-helidon for a standalone server, or zerozstack-server-jakarta to deploy a WAR. Start a standalone server with com.zeroz4j.server.Zeroz4jServer.start(port, appName) and never name a container in code: that call uses whichever binding module is on the classpath. zerozstack-server-vidocq is a second binding that needs Java 25 and serves the application's own @Path JAX-RS resources through Cassini, found at runtime among its beans (declare the resource and Application classes in a bean archive with META-INF/beans.xml); with both bindings on the classpath start-up fails unless -Dzeroz.server.binding=helidon or =vidocq picks one. A project generated from the archetype switches with 'mvn clean install -Pvidocq' or '-Phelidon', and the archetype's 'container' property (helidon by default) sets which is its default. Or generate a project from com.zeroz4j:zerozstack-archetype, which produces the shared/client/server module shape. Building from source is only needed when working on the framework itself.

A standalone server's main class (its main method, entry point or bootstrap) is one call: Zeroz4jServer.start(port, appName).join(), imported from com.zeroz4j.server. Read the port in your own main method (the examples use --port, then -Dzeroz.port, then a constant) and turn the development logins on only when asked, with --dev-login or -Dzeroz.security.mode=dev, never by default. Start-up fails with a sentence when no server binding or more than one is on the classpath. A WAR has no main class. See docs/guides/starting-the-server.md.

In a project generated from the archetype, choose the build command deliberately, because compiling the client for the browser is most of what a build costs. 'mvn compile' and 'mvn test-compile' run javac only and do NOT produce the browser bundle - use them for an ordinary check that the Java compiles, which is about a third of the time of a full build. 'mvn install' produces a readable, unoptimized bundle and a runnable application. 'mvn install -Pproduction' adds whole-program optimization and minification and is the shape that ships. Measured on a freshly generated project with a warm Maven cache: about 5 seconds for the quick check, 16 for a full install, 17 with -Pproduction; on a slow continuous-integration machine the full build is 60 to 90 seconds. Two consequences an assistant must plan around. First, the browser compiler accepts a smaller language than javac, so client code can pass the quick check and still fail to compile - run a full build before declaring client work finished, and give a pipeline 'mvn verify' rather than 'mvn test', which stops before the bundle is built. Second, minification renames things and has broken this framework before, so build and run -Pproduction before shipping rather than only at release time. Earlier versions of the archetype compiled the browser bundle on every build, always optimized and minified, which is what made an ordinary check slow.

Build with 'mvn clean install -DskipTests' from the repository root. Always include clean: each example server copies dependencies into target/libs, which is never pruned, so stale jars from earlier versions otherwise accumulate and cause duplicate-bean warnings at startup.

In a generated application, 'mvn install -Pproduction' also replaces the two CDN style tags in the client's src/main/webapp/index.html (Tailwind in the browser and daisyUI's full stylesheet) with one finished, minified local stylesheet, written to <app>-client/target/webapp-production together with a copy of index.html that links it; the server module serves that folder instead of src/main/webapp when -Pproduction is on, which covers Helidon, Vidocq, the Docker build and -Ppackage. The first such build downloads the pinned Tailwind 4.1.16 standalone executable and daisyUI 5.6.14 bundle once into ~/.zeroz4j/cache and checks their SHA-256, failing on a mismatch; the ordinary build stays on the CDN tags and downloads nothing. Do not remove the zeroz4j:styles:begin and zeroz4j:styles:end comments around the tags in index.html, because the build fails without them. A CSS class built by joining strings in application code is not found by the scanner; write it out whole. Application CSS goes in src/main/tailwind/app.css. The repository's own examples stay on the CDN tags.

The client compiles with TeaVM's JavaScript backend today. This is a deliberate interim choice because TeaVM's WasmGC backend does not yet provide functionality ZeroZ Stack needs; WasmGC is the intended destination, which is what the zerozstack-client module name refers to. Do not claim client code compiles to WebAssembly today, and do not change the JAVASCRIPT target.

There is no exec-maven-plugin. Run one of the seven original examples with: java -cp "target/classes;target/libs/*" com.zeroz4j.example.server.ExampleServer from its server module directory, using ':' instead of ';' on POSIX. payments-datamodels is started the same way but with com.zeroz4j.example.payments.server.ExampleServer. The examples added in 0.6.0 (routing-tour, oidc-login, scoped-signals, pwa-install) also build a runnable jar, so 'java -jar <example>-server/target/<example>-server-0.11.0.jar' works for those. 'mvn exec:java' does not work anywhere.

Several examples need a sign-in (chat-events, chat-livesync, job-monitor, components-showcase show a Login component; routing-tour and scoped-signals take ?user=admin&password=admin from the URL). todo-signals, form-signup, inventory-crud and payments-datamodels connect anonymously. Since 0.7.0 starting a server does NOT switch the built-in accounts on: pass --dev-login on the command line, which the run.bat scripts already do, or set -Dzeroz.security.mode=dev. Credentials are demo/demo (role user) and admin/admin (roles user and admin), validated by DevAuth from WebSocket handshake parameters. Replace this before any real deployment by registering an AuthenticationProvider.

Put @Secured and @RolesAllowed on the @RmiService interface and its methods, never on the implementing bean. The dispatcher scans only the interface, so annotations on the implementation are silently ignored and the method is left unprotected. These are com.zeroz4j.api.Secured and com.zeroz4j.api.RolesAllowed, not the Jakarta annotations of the same name.
Structure an application as three modules: shared (models and @RmiService interfaces), client (the UI, compiled for the browser by TeaVM), and server (CDI bean implementations).

Every type that crosses the wire must be annotated @DataModel. It may be a class with a public no-arg constructor plus a getter and setter for each serialized field; a record (0.8.0+), which needs none of that; or a sealed interface or sealed abstract class (0.8.0+) whose permitted types are each @DataModel and final. A record cannot be @LiveSync or @ClientWritable, cannot take part in a reference cycle, and cannot be a persistence root - use a class for any of those. A model may extend another @DataModel and the base class's fields travel with it (0.8.0+); extending a non-@DataModel class that has fields of its own, and shadowing a base field name, are both compile errors. The payments-datamodels example uses all three shapes in one working application and drives them through a real server in its test.

Declare RMI contracts as @RmiService interfaces in the shared module and implement them as @ApplicationScoped CDI beans in the server module. The client obtains a stub with new MyService_Stub(), generated by the annotation processor.

Bootstrap the client with Zeroz4jClient.connect(webSocketUrl, onReady). Do not call BinaryPackableRegistrar or WasmRmiClient.initialize directly; registrars are discovered automatically through META-INF/services.

Choose the state-propagation mechanism deliberately. Use a local ValueSignal for state that never leaves the browser tab. Use an RMI call for named operations and request/response, and a SlowCall when the work can pass 30 seconds. Use an EventTopic for discrete occurrences that carry no retained value. Use Signals.shared for one current value that late-joining clients must see. Use @LiveSync for an identified object whose fields are edited individually.
Never carry state in server events. Events have no retained value, no replay and no queueing, so a client that connects later or reconnects sees nothing. Use Signals.shared instead.

Client writes are denied by default. Opt in explicitly with Signals.sharedWritable or @ClientWritable. The server remains authoritative and re-checks role membership and validation annotations on every inbound write.

Model operations such as approve, checkout, delete or log in as RMI methods, not as LiveSync field edits. An operation deserves a name, its own @Secured and @RolesAllowed marks, and its own validation point. State edits sync, operations call.

SyncEngine.notifyChanged throws IllegalStateException unless the object has already been serialized to a client and therefore has an ObjectMapper handle. Return the object from an RMI method at least once before relying on LiveSync.

A @LiveSync object is a reactive dependency: read its getters inside Effect.create(...) and an inbound sync re-runs the effect automatically. Do not poll on a timer. Notification is per object, not per field.
Setters are the LiveSync tracking boundary. In-place collection edits such as obj.getTags().add(x) are invisible; reassign through the setter or call LiveMutationTracker.touch(obj) afterwards.

The server handles one connection's messages one at a time, in the order the client sent them (0.8.0+). Anything a browser sends after a @ClientWritable edit - an RMI call, a LiveMutex lock, a shared-signal write - is handled after that edit, so a service method sees the value the person actually typed. Do not generate a LiveMutex, a flush, or a retry to order one person's own messages; a lock is for two people editing the same object. Ordering is per connection, so a slow call for one user never delays another. Up to 32 messages may be waiting per connection (zeroz.ws.maxQueuedFramesPerSession, called zeroz.ws.maxConcurrentFramesPerSession before 0.8.0 and still read under that name); past that the connection is slowed down, never refused.

Do not wrap client event handlers in your own thread. Component.addDomEventListener already wraps every DOM listener via Component.threaded(...), so the handler body runs on a suspendable TeaVM green thread and a suspending RMI call works directly inside it. An extra thread is redundant and its UI updates may not repaint until the next event. For delayed work use Window.setTimeout. The browser refuses the clipboard, the microphone and the install prompt unless the call is made inside the click itself, so for those use Component.addGestureListener(type, listener), which runs on the event's own stack and must not call the server; Js.copyToClipboard(text, result) reports whether the copy worked. To make a remote call from a timer, a browser callback or an Effect use Background.run(task), Background.after(millis, task) or Background.every(millis, task) (com.zeroz4j.client), which return a Disposable for the repeating form and never overlap runs.
Dispose what you create. Effect.create and ServerEvents.on both return a Disposable, and Computed has dispose(). A view that creates them must release them when it is permanently removed.

Validation annotations (@NotBlank, @Min, @Max, @Size) are declared once on the model in the shared module. The generated MyModel_Rules class feeds client-side field feedback through field.withRule(...), and the server enforces the same rules independently on RMI arguments, LiveSync mutations and shared-signal writes. Client-side validation is user feedback only; the server's answer is the one that counts.

ZeroZ Stack is an experimental proof-of-concept at version 0.11.0, not a production framework. Field-level merging, version-conflict rejection, tracked collections and per-topic event subscription are not implemented. The @Route router, scoped signals, OpenID Connect sign-in, WAR deployment, file upload, records and sealed types on the wire, model inheritance, and an in-process test server are implemented.

Never empty a container by hand in client code. getElement().setInnerHTML("") takes the old screen off the page without telling it, so its timers and effects keep running. Use container.replaceContents(next), Component.replaceContents(element, next), removeAll() or remove(...); all of them run onDetach on everything leaving, however deeply nested (0.8.0+). If you wrote an onDetach before 0.8.0 and it never ran, it runs now.

Name a form field with withLabel("...") or setLabel("..."), never with the constructor argument: new TextField("x") sets the placeholder, which stops saying what the field is the moment somebody types and is announced by nothing. setHelperText, setRequiredIndicatorVisible and setErrorMessage put the other three pieces of text on the same field. Available on every input in the library since 0.8.0.

Ask for text by name, never by writing out a size and a fade (0.8.0+). com.zeroz4j.ui.theme.TextStyle has five: PAGE_TITLE, SECTION_TITLE, BODY, SECONDARY, CAPTION, used as TextStyle.SECONDARY.paragraph(text), TextStyle.CAPTION.span(text) or TextStyle.CAPTION.applyTo(component). How loud is a separate question answered by com.zeroz4j.ui.theme.Emphasis - FULL, QUIET, FAINT - passed as a second argument only where the text disagrees with its size, such as a small error line that must be read at full strength. Never write text-base-content/60 or any hand-picked opacity: that names a color and goes wrong on a tinted notice or a dark page. Text drawn inside a chart uses com.zeroz4j.ui.chart.PlotText - FIGURE, LABEL, CAPTION, MESSAGE - because stylesheet classes do not reach an SVG drawing; a build test fails if a chart draws text without naming a role.

The page is base-200 and a box on it is base-100 (0.11.0+). com.zeroz4j.api.ThemeBase sets those colors for the light and dark themes, in every shell the server sends, so do not write a theme file only to get a page and panels that differ. Never use bg-base-200 for a box or a sidebar: that is the page color. An application theme file outside a cascade layer wins over it.

Ask for a surface by name, never by writing out a background, border and shadow (0.11.0+). com.zeroz4j.ui.theme.Surface has six: PAGE, PANEL, TILE, SUNKEN, RAISED, OVERLAY, used as Surface.PANEL.applyTo(component) or Surface.TILE.div(). Never write bg-base-100 border border-base-300 shadow-sm rounded-box on a box: on a dark theme the page, the box and its edge are three near-identical grays and base-300 is darker than the box it outlines. A surface draws its edge and shadow from the text color, so it reads in light and dark, and it sets no padding and no layout. The stylesheet is added to the head the first time a surface is applied; --zeroz4j-surface-edge, --zeroz4j-surface-shade and --zeroz4j-surface-radius change it.

To run an application written for a servlet container (a WAR with servlets of its own) from the IDE or a test, use com.zeroz4j.server.dev.Zeroz4jDevServer from zerozstack-dev-tomcat: Zeroz4jDevServer.builder().port(8080).contextPath("/app").beans(MyServiceImpl.class).servlet(MyServlet.class).start(). It runs embedded Tomcat and Weld with no classpath scan, so every injected class has to be named in beans(...). Take the module with test or provided scope, never compile scope, and never put it in a deployed WAR. Do not hand-build Tomcat and Weld, and do not add a Tomcat dependency to a runtime module. Read docs/guides/war-dev-server.md first.

Anything a person clicks must be a Button, or a Link with a real href set through setHref/withHref/new Link(text, href). A click listener on a Div is unreachable by keyboard and announced as nothing; KeyboardAndNamingContractTest fails the build of zerozstack-ui-components for it. Menu.addItem builds a button and Menu.addLink builds a link. Put an overlay on a named layer with setLayer(Layer.TOAST) rather than picking a z-index; an open modal Dialog sits in the browser's top layer, which no number can reach.

Test a server in-process with the zerozstack-server-test artifact at test scope (0.8.0+). TestServer.builder().named(...).beans(YourServiceImpl.class).start() starts one in about a tenth of a second; server.connect(user, roles) gives a TestConnection the server treats as a real browser, and every read on it waits for the server's writer first. Close both with try-with-resources. A call driven in as a frame with browser.send(bytes) is queued and handled on another thread, so its answer arrives a moment later and is not necessarily the last frame: wait, and match the message number the request was sent under. Each server owns its own connections, disclosures and settings, so two can run side by side; builder().ignoringSystemProperties().set(ServerSettings.X, v) gives one server settings the process does not have.

The server accepts binary messages up to 4 MB by default (zeroz.ws.maxBinaryMessageBytes, 0.7.0+). A larger message closes the connection instead of raising an error the application can catch, because @OnMessage takes a whole message. Never send file contents through an RMI call. One connection may also have at most 32 messages being handled at once and 256 messages or 8 MB waiting to go out; an empty outgoing queue always accepts the next message however large.

Accept files with the FileUpload component on the client and an @ApplicationScoped class implementing com.zeroz4j.server.FileUploadHandler on the server; the framework discovers it and hands it each finished file as an UploadedFile. Several kinds of upload each get a handler: override getKind() and getMaxBytes() in the handler and call setKind on the FileUpload; a box with no kind reaches the handler whose kind is empty. Files go over their own HTTP address (zeroz4j-upload), not the RMI socket, and 25 MB per file is the default (zeroz.upload.maxBytes, zeroz.upload.maxBytes.<kind> per kind); files are streamed to disk in 64 KB pieces, so a 100 MB recording does not cost 100 MB of memory. The temporary file is deleted the moment the handler returns, so move or copy it inside the method. getFileName() and getContentType() are text the browser sent: generate the stored name yourself and check the bytes if the type matters. A WAR needs zerozstack-server-jakarta and a standalone server needs zerozstack-server-jaxrs; both already carry the address.

Serve a file the server holds with an @ApplicationScoped class implementing com.zeroz4j.server.FileDownloadHandler (getKind(), open(DownloadRequest) returning FileDownload.of(path), notFound() or forbidden()). The page calls AudioPlayer.setServerFile(kind, id) or VideoPlayer.setServerFile(kind, id); the framework issues an address at zeroz4j-download tied to the browser and the signed-in connection, calls the handler on every request, and answers byte ranges so media can seek. Never put file bytes in an RMI result. Audio, video, pictures other than SVG, PDF and plain text are sent inline and everything else as attachment. EmbeddedFrame shows another page and takes the height the page reports; the page needs com.zeroz4j.api.EmbeddedFrameScript.HEIGHT_SCRIPT, which setContent adds. A sandbox without allow-scripts stops that script.

A live change is checked against every object it reaches, not only the outermost one (0.7.0+). A @LiveSync model nested inside a @ClientWritable model needs its own @ClientWritable and its own roles, and one refusal refuses the whole change with a message beginning 'The change also alters a'.

A client may read an object back, or take a LiveMutex lock on it, only when the server actually sent that object to that browser (0.7.0+). The server keeps a record per browser holding 10,000 objects, dropped after 24 hours idle (zeroz.disclosure.maxHandlesPerClient, zeroz.disclosure.idleHours). Knowing an object's handle is not enough. Ask the same question in a service with Disclosures.wasDisclosedTo(session, handleId). A LiveMutex caller waits 30 seconds (zeroz.livemutex.waitSeconds) and callers are served in arrival order.

Since 0.7.0 an unexpected server exception reaches the client as 'The server could not complete this request. Reference: <code>', with the real message and stack trace in the server log under the same code. To send a sentence the caller should read, throw com.zeroz4j.server.ClientVisibleException. The framework's own refusals - authentication required, access denied, unknown service, unknown method, failed validation - still travel word for word.

Do not write a loading spinner, a navigation wrapper, or click and popstate listeners for routing feedback. An application gets both with no call at all: a top bar, a centered spinner card and a wait cursor once any navigation has run 300 ms, hidden when the latest navigation finishes or fails with no timeout of its own (Router.showBusyIndicator(false) to opt out), and a plain message with a Retry button when the latest navigation fails (Router.showFailureMessage(false) to opt out). Turn one off only when the application already renders its own. Style both with the --zeroz4j-busy-* and --zeroz4j-failure-* CSS custom properties. For a custom indicator use Router.addLifecycleListener: every navigation raises started, and the one started last always ends in exactly one finished or failed; an older navigation it overtook raises nothing more. Router.onError adds a handler rather than replacing the previous one (Router.addErrorListener returns a Disposable). A failed navigation is never re-run by itself after a reconnect; Router.retry() re-runs it. RmiSecurityContext.onAuthenticated and onResolved run again after every reconnect, so start the router and register its listeners once.

Do not write reconnect plumbing. Since 0.5.0 the framework reconnects with backoff, shows a built-in outage banner (Zeroz4jClient.showConnectionBanner(false) to opt out), re-subscribes shared signals, re-syncs live objects in place, and queues offline signal writes and @ClientWritable edits for flush on reconnect. Connection state is a signal: WasmRmiClient.connectionState(). Since 0.9.1 it does not reconnect while the page is hidden, resets the backoff only after a connection stayed open 30 seconds, and stops after 10 failures in a row: the state is then CLOSED with WasmRmiClientChannel.hasGivenUp() true, and the built-in bar asks the person to reload. An application drawing its own indicator must handle that state too.

Never add maven-shade-plugin to a ZeroZ Stack server. Weld treats each jar as a separate bean archive and a merged jar breaks CDI discovery (beans vanish or WELD-001409 duplicates). To package: mvn verify -Ppackage produces a self-contained jpackage folder with a launcher executable and bundled runtime; the generated Dockerfile builds a layered container image; both keep every jar intact on a plain classpath. On Linux never use a bare libs/* classpath wildcard: it expands in arbitrary order and one ordering registers Helidon's WebSocket routing too late, so every WebSocket handshake answers 404 while HTTP works. Sort it: java -cp "target/classes:$(ls target/libs/*.jar | sort | tr '\n' ':')" ... (the generated Dockerfile already sorts).

RMI calls fail immediately with DisconnectedException while the connection is down, and are never queued or replayed automatically. A connection that dies without closing is noticed by the keepalive: a call waiting five seconds with nothing arriving triggers a ping, and a ping unanswered for ten seconds closes the socket so its calls fail with DisconnectedException (Keepalive.configureLiveness(seconds), 0 turns it off). A call the server never answers fails at the request timeout (30 s, WasmRmiClient.setRequestTimeout) with RequestTimeoutException, on a timer of its own. Do not write heartbeats or watchdog timers. Catch either exception to retry, or disable controls while connectionState() is not CONNECTED. Session ids change on every reconnect: re-register anything keyed by session id from a StateListener on CONNECTED, and observe the CDI event SessionClosedEvent on the server to clean up stale entries.

A @DataModel may declare EclipseStore Lazy<T> fields. The reference travels as a session-scoped handle and never as its contents; the client resolves it with a suspending RMI round trip on first get(), and the result is cached. Lazy references originate on the server, so a client cannot create one and send it up - assign the resolved value instead.

Never mutate a signal's value in place. ValueSignal.set skips notification when the new value equals the old one, so mutating a list and setting it back changes nothing. Use update() and return a new instance.

As of 0.4.0 these fail loudly rather than silently: SyncEngine.notifyChanged on an object never serialized to a client throws; an unserializable event or shared-signal payload throws to the caller; a conflicting shared-signal declaration throws; bindValue with a non-writable signal throws (use bindValueReadOnly for one-way); and @ClientWritable without @LiveSync, or on a field with no setter, is a compile error.
A rejected LiveSync mutation sends the writer a 0x15 REJECT frame naming the model and the reason, in addition to the corrective sync. Do not assume a reverted change is unexplained.

The annotation processor rejects unsupported @DataModel field types at compile time and names the replacement: object arrays (use a List), ZonedDateTime/OffsetDateTime/ZoneId/Period (use Instant, LocalDate or a String), java.util.Date (use Instant), and concrete collections outside the rebuilt hierarchy such as TreeSet, TreeMap and LinkedList (declare the field as Set, Map or List). ArrayList, HashSet and HashMap are fine.

Server events and shared signals reach every connected session by default. Scope events explicitly for anything belonging to somebody: events.publishToUser(topic, payload, principalName) or events.publishToSession(topic, payload, sessionId). LiveSync scopes the same way via syncEngine.notifyChanged(obj, Scope.SESSION or Scope.USER, target). Shared signals cannot be scoped at all -- a shared signal is one value the whole server agrees on, so per-user state is not a shared signal.

To replace the development authentication, implement com.zeroz4j.server.AuthenticationProvider and register it in META-INF/services/com.zeroz4j.server.AuthenticationProvider. It is discovered via ServiceLoader, not CDI, because the handshake runs before the endpoint exists. Return an AuthenticatedPrincipal with a name, roles and optionally a tenant; return null to leave the connection anonymous. Registering a provider disables the DevAuth fallback.

Scope.TENANT filters on the tenant an AuthenticationProvider attached to the session. A session with no tenant never matches, so a connection that did not sign in receives nothing sent that way. Read the tenant in a service with RmiRequestContext.getTenantId().

Set zeroz.clientId.secret to a long random string, the same on every node, in any real deployment: unset, the key that signs the browser id is regenerated at every startup. Set zeroz.hosts to the host names the deployment answers for; unset, a handshake addressed to any name is accepted. Leave zeroz.origins unset unless the page is served from a different host than the socket. Every zeroz.* setting and its default is listed in docs/guides/packaging.md.

Persistence runs on ZeroZ DB (com.zeroz4j:zerozdb). Inject ZeroZDbNode and send a DbCommand to write: everything the command enlists with ctx.edit/ctx.store lands in ONE atomic commit, and a command that throws persists nothing and restores the objects in memory. The same command runs wherever the data is, so zeroz4j.store.mode = EMBEDDED | AUTO_SERVER | CLIENT is a deployment choice rather than an application one.

DbCommand and DbQuery implementations must be plain classes with public fields and a public no-arg constructor, never records: EclipseStore's serializer reaches fields directly and the JVM refuses that for records without --add-exports java.base/jdk.internal.misc=ALL-UNNAMED. It fails at the first remote call, not at compile time.

The rules for the exact version an application depends on ship inside its jars. zerozstack-shared-api carries META-INF/zeroz4j/AGENTS.md, generated during the framework build from this rule list and stamped with that build's version; every application resolves that artifact. Read it with 'unzip -p ~/.m2/repository/com/zeroz4j/zerozstack-shared-api/<version>/zerozstack-shared-api-<version>.jar META-INF/zeroz4j/AGENTS.md'. The documentation for that version is in the same jar, under META-INF/zeroz4j/docs/ with the folder layout of docs/. A project generated from zerozstack-archetype also gets its own AGENTS.md at its root, naming the same version. Prefer both to any documentation index when they disagree: an index follows the framework's main line and describes features an older project does not have.

To answer in the caller's language, declare .properties files in the shared module (i18n/app.properties for the fallback language, i18n/app_de.properties for German) and mark them with an empty class annotated @MessageCatalog(baseName = "i18n/app", fallback = "en"). The annotation processor writes AppText_Text with one method per key, camel-cased, taking one argument per {0} blank; each returns a Message, not a String, so the sentence can be carried out to the edge of the server and rendered there. Throw new ClientVisibleException(AppText_Text.x(...)) to refuse in the caller's language while the server log keeps English; the String constructor stays correct for a one-language application. Blanks are {0}, {1} and nothing else - never MessageFormat, which costs 43% more browser download. The connection's language is resolved once at the handshake (lang parameter, zeroz-lang cookie, Accept-Language, zeroz.i18n.defaultLocale, then en), narrowed to the languages the deployment has files for, and read with RmiRequestContext.getLocale(), never from a method argument. Add one test calling CatalogParity.assertConsistent(folder, baseName): nothing else checks the other languages. English is unchanged for a project that adds no language.

In the browser, the words for the connection's language arrive on the AUTH frame before the first screen is built, so there is nothing to fetch and nothing to configure. THE ONE RULE: call Message.text() INSIDE an Effect - new Button(AppText_Text.taskAdd().text()) reads the words once and the label never changes again when somebody switches language. Write Effect.create(() -> button.setText(AppText_Text.taskAdd().text())) instead. MessageReadContractTest fails the build on a read outside an effect; @ReadsMessagesOnce on the method is the escape hatch for a read that really is once-only. It cannot see a read one ordinary method call deep, words stored in a variable inside an effect and used outside it, or English left hard-coded - do not trust it further than that. Hold a Message, not a String, when a value is stored and drawn later. Add new LanguageSelector() for a picker: it offers only the languages the deployment has words for, binds itself, and is a real select element so the keyboard works. Register ClientMessages.useFallback(AppText_Catalog.BASE_NAME, AppText_Catalog::lookup) once at start-up for screens drawn before the connection is up. Switching language rebuilds nothing: a half-filled form keeps its values.

Formats.number(), currency(), date() and friends are the ONLY door in ZeroZ Stack to java.text, and the first call from a client module adds 233 KB to the bundle and 43 KB gzipped to every visitor's download, with about 6 KB gzipped more per locale named in java.util.Locale.available. Translating an interface into twenty languages costs the browser nothing, because the words travel over the connection; formatting one number the local way costs more than all of them together. Do not reach for it casually, never let framework code call it, and set java.util.Locale.available and java.util.Locale.default in the client module's teavm-maven-plugin properties when you do - java.util.Locale.default MUST contain an underscore (en_US), or the application dies at class initialization with nothing useful to read. There are no plural rules: {0} tasks left says 1 tasks left, so write two keys and an if.

Do not hand-write browser helpers. com.zeroz4j.ui.Browser has storageGet/storageSet/storageRemove (tolerate blocked storage), open, goTo, path, scrollToBottom, scrollIntoView, download (hidden link) and warn. For input use DateField (LocalDate), TimeField (LocalTime) and NumberField (Double) with withLabel, never a TextField parsed by hand. For a plain element use El, for a router link RouteLink(path, text).setCurrent(boolean) in com.zeroz4j.client.router, for a Select whose value differs from its text Select.setOptions(map). Icon has lock, mic, calendar, bell, user, mail, download, eye and more; Icon.ofShapes draws your own. Pwa.pushState() and Pwa.deviceLabel() answer what a settings screen needs before asking for notification permission. Chart series colors follow --color-chart-1 to --color-chart-8 in your theme CSS.

Application with its own accounts: write one @ApplicationScoped com.zeroz4j.server.SignInHandler (signIn checks the password and returns an AuthenticatedPrincipal or null; resume returns the current principal for a valid session, or null to end it) and put new Login() on the screen (0.11.0+). That turns on POST zeroz4j-session/sign-in, sign-out and renew under Helidon, in a WAR and on Vidocq. Do not generate a sign-in servlet, a session cookie, a return-page check, a cross-site check, attempt limiting or a renewal timer: the framework does all of them. Sign out in the browser with SignInSession.signOut(). End access with SignInSessions.current().revokeUser(name, tenantId, reason), which closes live connections, but that record is in memory, so anything that must survive a restart goes in resume, for example session.startedAt() against the time of the last password change. The cookie is read after any AuthenticationProvider, so it works beside OIDC and the development logins.

Login is a real HTML form with name and autocomplete on both fields. new Login() posts natively, so password managers fill it and browsers offer to save it, and it needs no listener. new Login(listener) hands the values to code and stays on the page. Never write a sign-in form by hand, and never add a keydown listener for Enter: pressing Enter already submits the form.

Keep secrets and settings in the application's property file, zeroz4j.properties in the working directory, outside the jar and out of version control (0.11.0+). -Dzeroz.settings.file names another file, and a -D beats the file. Environment variables are not read, so do not generate code that reads them. Set zeroz.signin.secret to at least 32 random characters in any real deployment: unset, every restart signs everybody out, and shorter is refused. Never reuse zeroz.clientId.secret for it.

To leave application state on a connection at the handshake, return principal.withAttribute(name, value) from an AuthenticationProvider or SignInHandler.resume, and read it in a service with RmiRequestContext.getSessionAttribute(name) (0.11.0+). It never goes to the browser, and it ends with the connection, so set it at every handshake. Do not build a registry keyed by session id for this.

Injecting EmbeddedStorageManager still works but only where the data is local, and it pins the application to EMBEDDED or AUTO_SERVER mode; in CLIENT mode it fails with an explanation. With the raw manager, each store() call is a separate commit - use storage.storeAll(a, b) so a crash cannot persist one object and lose the other.
